title: Bread and water
hookLine: Epicurus said plain bread and water, when hungry, give the highest pleasure (Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laërtius 10)
tomorrow: Where death is, I am not

lines: NOT SPECIAL WATER. A THIRSTY DRINKER.
cards: The best glass of water is rarely the fanciest. It comes after a long hike, or a fever, or a day of moving furniture in August. The water isn't special.
The drinker is thirsty. That's the whole secret, and Epicurus wrote it down in a letter to a friend named Menoeceus.
The letter survives because Diogenes Laërtius copied it into his Lives, and it's short enough to read in one sitting.

teach.b: First, the claim. In the Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus says that plain food gives as much pleasure as an expensive meal, once the pain of hunger is taken away.
Then the line people remember: bread and water give the highest pleasure when someone who needs them puts them to their lips. Second, the reasoning.
Epicurus sorted desires into kinds. Some are natural and necessary, like food when you're hungry, rest when you're tired, friends. Some are natural but not necessary, like fancy food.
And some are neither, like fame or endless wealth, and those, he said, have no natural limit. The first kind is easy to satisfy. That's good news.
Third, the training. He doesn't say luxury is evil. He says getting used to simple living makes you healthy, makes you unafraid of losing things, and makes the occasional feast taste better.
Someone who's content with bread and water can't be threatened much by fortune.
The Greek for that is autarkeia, self-sufficiency. Fourth, the week.

teach.h: THE WEEK: NEIGHBORS ON THE PORCH.
teach.b: The porch had many neighbors. Posidonius found order in the tides. Cicero wrote duties for his son.
Scipio saw Rome from the stars. Musonius called marriage a partnership. Hipparchia chose a cloak and an argument.
And Epicurus, from his garden, offers a plain teaching: what a body needs is easy to get, and plain bread tastes like a feast to someone who is actually hungry.

how: Epicureans practice simple eating, often choosing plain food and enjoying it fully, as training in needing little and fearing loss less.

games.q: you're hungry after a long day. a friend offers either plain bread or a costly feast. what does Epicurus say?
o: the plain bread gives as much pleasure, once hunger is gone.
games.why: Epicurus says plain fare gives as much pleasure as luxury once the pain of want is removed, and bread and water give the highest pleasure to the hungry.

practice: If you have a glass of water nearby, notice your thirst first, then take one slow sip and follow it the whole way down: cold, plain, real. Take another, just as slowly, and notice it's a full pleasure that cost almost nothing.
If you have no water, breathe instead, and notice that the breath is plain and good, too.

wordCard.voice: Autarkeia. Epicurus's word for self-sufficiency: being content with little, so fortune has less power to frighten you. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: self-sufficiency. Epicurus calls it a great good in the Letter to Menoeceus.

carryVoice: Your line: hard to frighten. Need little, and fortune has little to take. A week of neighbors, complete.
